title: Frequency and period (f = 1/T)
keyIdea: Frequency f is the number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz): 1 Hz is one wave per second. The time period T is the time for one whole wave, in seconds. They are reciprocals: f = 1 ÷ T and T = 1 ÷ f, so f × T = 1. A period of 0.02 s gives 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz. A 440 Hz sound has T = 1 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.0023 s. Double the frequency and the period halves. Always put T in seconds before using f = 1/T: 20 ms is 0.02 s.
familyTip: Time 10 swings of a pendulum or a child on a swing with a phone stopwatch. Divide by 10 to get the period of one swing, then work out 1 ÷ T for the frequency. Try a shorter string or a smaller push and compare.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: set waves per second, fill an f and T table, drag one wave to 0.02 s, tune 440 Hz and match periods to frequencies.

kid: Frequency f is how many waves pass a point each second. Its unit is the hertz, Hz. 1 Hz means one wave each second, and 50 Hz means fifty.
The time period T is the time for one whole wave, crest to crest, in seconds. If 4 waves pass each second, each one takes a quarter of a second: T = 0.25 s.
So f and T are reciprocals: f = 1 ÷ T and T = 1 ÷ f. Multiply them and you always get 1. When the frequency doubles, the period halves.
Put T in seconds first. A period of 20 ms is 0.02 s, so f = 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz. A 440 Hz note has T = 1 ÷ 440, about 0.0023 s or 2.3 ms.
adult: Ages 13 to 15. GCSE physics (AQA 4.6.1.2) defines frequency as the number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz, and requires period = 1 / frequency, T = 1/f. The KS3 programme introduces frequency in hertz for sound and other waves. Key words: frequency, hertz (Hz), time period, oscillation, cycle, reciprocal, millisecond.

Common mistakes: treating frequency and period as the same number (T = 0.25 s so f = 0.25 Hz); thinking frequency and period rise together; reading 1 Hz as a length or a height; using milliseconds in f = 1/T (1 ÷ 20 = 0.05 Hz instead of 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz); decimal slips such as 1 ÷ 50 = 0.5; and multiplying instead of dividing (T = 440 s).

A quick check: f × T must equal 1 when T is in seconds. Estimating first helps too: many waves each second means each wave lasts well under a second. Frequency sets the pitch of a sound and the colour of light, and the period is what an oscilloscope trace shows from crest to crest.

In the lab students set a wave to 4 waves per second and see each wave last 0.25 s, fill a table for 1, 2, 4, 5 and 10 Hz, drag the end of one wave on a 0.1 s axis to T = 0.02 s and read 50 Hz, tune a 10 ms trace to 440 Hz, then match periods (including 20 ms) to frequencies with decoys for the usual slips.

practice.prompt: What does a frequency of 1 Hz mean?
practice.hint: The hertz is a unit of 'per second'.
practice.explain: 1 Hz is one wave, or one cycle, each second. Length is wavelength and height is amplitude.

practice.prompt: {=k*s} waves pass a point in {s} seconds. What is the frequency in Hz?
practice.hint: Frequency is waves per second. Divide the number of waves by the time.
practice.explain: {=k*s} waves ÷ {s} s = {k} waves each second, so f = {k} Hz.

practice.prompt: A wave has a frequency of {=((a*a+a+2)/2)*(8*b*b-4*b+1)} Hz. What is its period in seconds?
practice.hint: T = 1 ÷ f. Check that f × T comes to 1.

practice.prompt: A wave has a period of 0.02 s. What is its frequency in Hz?
practice.hint: Use f = 1 ÷ T with T in seconds.

practice.prompt: A wave's frequency doubles. What happens to its period?
practice.hint: f × T = 1. If f gets twice as big, what must T do?
practice.explain: T = 1 ÷ f, so twice the frequency means half the period: 5 Hz to 10 Hz takes T from 0.2 s to 0.1 s.

pool.prompt: A wave has a period of 0.25 s. What is its frequency in Hz?
pool.hint: How many quarter-seconds fit in one second?
pool.explain: f = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 Hz: four waves each second.

pool.prompt: Calculate the period of a 440 Hz sound, in seconds. Give 2 significant figures.
pool.hint: Use T = 1 ÷ f, then round to 2 significant figures.
pool.explain: T = 1 ÷ 440 = 0.00227… s, which is 0.0023 s to 2 significant figures, about 2.3 ms.

pool.prompt: A wave has a period of 20 ms. What is its frequency?
pool.hint: Change 20 ms into seconds before using f = 1 ÷ T.
pool.explain: 20 ms = 0.02 s, and 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50 Hz. Using 20 instead of 0.02 gives the wrong 0.05 Hz.

pool.prompt: A wave has a frequency of {f} Hz. How many waves pass a point in {t} seconds?
pool.hint: {f} Hz means {f} waves pass each second. Multiply by the number of seconds.

pool.prompt: UK mains electricity has a frequency of 50 Hz. What is its period?
pool.hint: T = 1 ÷ 50. Check your answer by multiplying it by 50.
pool.explain: T = 1 ÷ 50 = 0.02 s, and 50 × 0.02 = 1. 0.5 s is a decimal slip; 50 s multiplies instead of divides.

pool.prompt: On a displacement-time graph, the time from one crest to the next crest is…
pool.hint: The horizontal axis is time. One crest to the next is one whole wave.
pool.explain: The time for one whole wave is the period. Frequency is 1 ÷ that time; wavelength is a distance, read from a distance graph.

pool.prompt: A buoy bobs up and down {n} times in {=2*n} seconds. What is the frequency in Hz?
pool.hint: Frequency is waves per second: number of waves ÷ time.
pool.explain: {n} ÷ {=2*n} = 0.5, so f = 0.5 Hz. Each bob takes 2 s, and 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5.

pool.prompt: Wave A is 100 Hz and wave B is 200 Hz. Which has the longer period?
pool.hint: Fewer waves each second means each wave lasts longer.
pool.explain: T = 1 ÷ 100 = 0.01 s for A and 1 ÷ 200 = 0.005 s for B. The lower frequency has the longer period.
